Entering a denser medium, light slows - and since the **frequency is fixed**, the
wavelength must shrink with it.
**Step 1 — recall what Huygens' construction gives.** The secondary wavelets advance
more slowly in the denser medium:
v = **c/µ** ✓ so with µ > 1 the **speed decreases** ✓
**Step 2 — recall what cannot change.** The **frequency** ✓ It is set by the **source**,
and the boundary cannot create or destroy wave crests - as many arrive per second as
leave.
**Step 3 — deduce the wavelength.** From v = fλ, with f fixed,
λ ∝ **v** ✓ so the **wavelength also decreases**:
λ_medium = **λ₀/µ** ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** **Wavelength and speed both decrease** ✓
**A worked instance.** Yellow light, λ₀ = 589 nm, entering glass of µ = 1·5:
v = 3 x 10⁸/1·5 = **2 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹** ✓
λ = 589/1·5 = **393 nm** ✓
f = 2 x 10⁸/393 x 10⁻⁹ = **5·09 x 10¹⁴ Hz** ✓ unchanged, as required.
**Why frequency is the invariant.** Wave crests are **conserved** at a boundary ✓ If
f differed on the two sides, crests would pile up or vanish there - impossible for a
continuous field.
**Why the colour does not change under water.** Colour is determined by **frequency**,
not wavelength ✓ which is why objects look the same colour to a diver even though the
light's wavelength inside the water is shorter by a third.
**How Snell's law follows.** The wavefront pivots at the boundary because one end
advances more slowly:
sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂ = **µ₂/µ₁** ✓
and bending **towards** the normal in the denser medium follows at once.
**The contrast with Newton's theory.** Corpuscles were supposed to speed **up** on
entering glass ✓ **Foucault**'s 1850 measurement in water found the speed **lower**,
deciding the matter in Huygens' favour.
**Where this changes the physics of an experiment.** Young's slits immersed in water
give fringes **narrower** by 1/µ, since β = λD/d with λ shortened ✓ a direct and
measurable consequence.
**Why the amplitude also falls.** Part of the light is **reflected** at the boundary ✓
about 4% at an air-glass surface at normal incidence, which is why lenses are coated.
**Reading the distractors.** Any option in which the two **move oppositely** ✗ violates
the constancy of f, since v = fλ forces them to change together ✓ The option in which
both **increase** ✗ describes passing into a **rarer** medium.
∴ Wavelength and speed decrease.

For the echoes to come at **equal** intervals the man must stand **midway**, and then
the gap between echoes is the time for sound to cross and return over half the gap.
**Step 1 — set up.** Let the cliffs be D apart and the man x from one of them ✓
**Step 2 — write the two echo times.**
from the near cliff: **2x/v** ✓
from the far cliff: **2(D − x)/v** ✓
**Step 3 — impose equal intervals.** A **uniform** series requires the two to be equal:
2x/v = 2(D − x)/v, so **x = D/2** ✓ the man stands midway.
**Step 4 — use the one-second interval.**
2x/v = 1
x = v/2 = **170 m** ✓
**Step 5 — find the separation.**
D = 2x = **340 m** ✓
**Why a series of echoes is heard at all, not just two.** The sound bounces **back and
forth** between the cliffs ✓ Each round trip takes 2D/v = **2 s**, and in that time one
echo arrives from each cliff - so the ear receives a steady train one second apart,
fading as energy is lost at each reflection.
**The check on the pattern.** With x = 170 m, echoes arrive at
**1 s** (near cliff), **2 s** (far cliff), **3 s**, **4 s** ... ✓ exactly the uniform
series described.
**Why standing off-centre breaks the pattern.** The intervals would **alternate** -
short, long, short, long ✓ With x = 100 m, echoes come at 0·59 s and 1·41 s, then repeat
every 2 s: a limping rhythm, not a regular one.
**Why the sound must travel twice the distance.** An echo goes **to** the cliff and
**back** ✓ Forgetting the factor of 2 is the standard error and gives 680 m.
**Why a clap is used.** It is a **sharp, brief** sound ✓ so the echoes are separated in
time rather than smeared into one another. A sustained shout would give reverberation
instead of distinct echoes.
**The minimum distance for a distinguishable echo.** The ear resolves sounds about
**0·1 s** apart, needing 2d = 340 x 0·1, so **d = 17 m** ✓ which is why a small room
gives reverberation and a cliff face a clean echo.
**Where the energy goes.** Each reflection loses some to absorption and scattering ✓ so
the train of echoes dies away after a few repetitions.
**Reading the distractors.** **680 m** ✗ forgets to halve for the return journey.
**1700 m** ✗ and **1620 m** ✗ correspond to intervals of 5 s and about 4·8 s ✓
∴ 340 m.

Loudness is governed by **intensity**; pitch by **frequency**.
**Step 1 — take loudness.** It is the **sensation** produced by the wave's energy ✓ and
depends chiefly on the **intensity**,
I ∝ **a²** ✓ the square of the amplitude.
**Step 2 — take pitch.** The sensation of highness or lowness ✓ determined by the
**frequency**: a high note is a high frequency.
**Step 3 — conclude.** **Intensity and frequency** ✓
**The three characteristics of a musical note, and their physical correlates.**
**loudness** ← **intensity** ✓
**pitch** ← **frequency** ✓
**quality (timbre)** ← the **number and relative intensity of the harmonics** ✓
It is the third that lets the ear distinguish a violin from a flute sounding the same
note equally loudly.
**Why loudness is not simply intensity.** The ear's response is roughly **logarithmic** -
the **Weber-Fechner** law ✓ which is why loudness is measured in **decibels**,
L = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀) ✓ with I₀ = 10⁻¹² W m⁻². Ten times the intensity sounds only about
twice as loud.
**Why the ear's sensitivity depends on frequency too.** It is most sensitive around
**2-4 kHz** ✓ so a 100 Hz tone needs far more intensity than a 3 kHz tone to seem
equally loud. Strictly, loudness depends on **both** - but intensity is the primary
factor, and frequency is already the answer for pitch.
**The audible range.** About **20 Hz to 20 kHz** ✓ narrowing with age from the top.
Below is infrasound, above ultrasound.
**Why velocity is irrelevant.** The speed of sound in air depends on **temperature**
alone, not on the note ✓ All frequencies travel at the same 340 m s⁻¹ - which is
fortunate, or an orchestra heard from the back of a hall would arrive out of order.
**The relation that ties them.** v = fλ ✓ With v fixed, a higher pitch means a shorter
**wavelength**: 20 Hz gives 17 m, 20 kHz gives 1·7 cm.
**Why the number of harmonics is the wrong answer for pitch.** It fixes the **quality** ✓
A note's pitch is set by its **fundamental**, which is why a trumpet and a clarinet
playing middle C sound the same pitch but unmistakably different.
**Reading the distractors.** Each pairs the right quantity for one characteristic with
the wrong one for the other ✓ Matching loudness to intensity and pitch to frequency
settles it.
∴ intensity and frequency.

The siren's frequency is **holes x revolutions per second**.
**Step 1 — convert the speed.**
360 rpm = 360/60 = **6 revolutions per second** ✓
**Step 2 — count the puffs.** Each revolution sends **60** puffs of air through the
holes ✓
**Step 3 — multiply.**
f = 60 x 6
= **360 Hz** ✓
**Why "in unison" means equal frequency.** Two sources in unison produce **no beats** ✓
so their frequencies are identical - here 360 Hz, the fork's frequency.
**How a siren produces a note.** A jet of air plays on a rotating perforated disc ✓ Each
time a hole passes the jet, a puff escapes; the regular train of puffs is a periodic
pressure wave, and the ear hears it as a tone.
**Why the note rises as the disc speeds up.** f = nN with n the holes and N the
revolutions per second ✓ Doubling the speed to 720 rpm gives **720 Hz** - an octave
higher. The rising wail of an accelerating siren is exactly this.
**Why this is a useful instrument.** It generates a note of **known, calculable**
frequency from a measured rotation rate ✓ which is how Seebeck and later Savart
determined the frequencies of tuning forks and the limits of hearing, before electronic
oscillators existed.
**A check in the audible range.** 360 Hz lies between F♯ and G above middle C ✓
comfortably audible, as the question requires.
**The common slip.** Using 360 rpm **directly** as 360 Hz ✓ It gives the right number
here only by coincidence - 60 holes and 60 seconds cancel. With 30 holes the answer
would be **180 Hz**, and the slip would show.
**The general formula.**
f = **n x (rpm)/60** ✓
**Why the hole size does not matter.** It affects the **loudness** and the **quality** of
the note - the harmonic content - but not the fundamental frequency ✓ which is fixed by
how often a hole passes the jet.
**Beats, if the two were slightly different.** A fork of 356 Hz would give **4 beats per
second** ✓ which is how a siren is tuned to a fork: slow the disc until the beats vanish.
**Reading the distractors.** **10 Hz** ✗ is 600/60, a confusion of units. **6 Hz** ✗ is
the revolution rate alone. **216 kHz** ✗ multiplies 60 by 360 by 10 ✓
∴ 360 Hz.

On a sonometer with the tension fixed, **f ∝ 1/l**.
**Step 1 — write the law of lengths.**
f = (1/2l)√(T/m) ✓ so with T and m constant,
**f₁l₁ = f₂l₂** ✓
**Step 2 — substitute.**
256 x 25 = f₂ x 16 ✓
**Step 3 — solve.**
f₂ = 6400/16
= **400 Hz** ✓
**Why the frequency rises as the length falls.** A shorter string has a shorter
**wavelength** for its fundamental, λ = 2l ✓ and with the wave speed unchanged, f = v/λ
must rise. Stopping a violin string higher up the fingerboard raises the note for
exactly this reason.
**The wave speed here, as a check.**
v = fλ = 256 x 2(0·25) = **128 m s⁻¹** ✓
and for the second fork: 400 x 2(0·16) = **128 m s⁻¹** ✓ the same, as it must be - the
speed depends on tension and mass per unit length, neither of which changed.
**The three laws of a vibrating string.**
**length**: f ∝ 1/l ✓
**tension**: f ∝ √T ✓
**mass per unit length**: f ∝ 1/√m ✓
all contained in f = (1/2l)√(T/m), **Mersenne's** law.
**How resonance is detected in practice.** A small paper **rider** is placed on the
wire ✓ When the length is adjusted to resonance, the rider is thrown off violently -
a far more sensitive indicator than listening.
**Why the tension must be kept constant.** It appears as √T ✓ A 1% change in tension
shifts the frequency by 0·5%, enough to spoil the measurement - which is why the weight
hanging over the pulley is left untouched between the two trials.
**What the sonometer is for.** Verifying these laws, and **measuring** the frequency of
an unknown fork against a known one ✓ exactly the use here.
**A musical check.** 400/256 = **1·5625** ✓ a little more than a perfect fifth (1·5), so
the second fork sounds about eight semitones above the first.
**Why the string's material does not enter the ratio.** It is the **same** wire in both
trials, so m cancels ✓ Only the ratio of lengths matters.
**Reading the distractors.** **163·84 Hz** ✗ is 256 x 16/25, the ratio **inverted** - the
commonest error. **320 Hz** ✗ and **204·8 Hz** ✗ match no consistent ratio ✓
∴ 400 Hz.

Filing a prong **raises** its frequency, so the fork must have started **below** B.
**Step 1 — use the beat frequency.** 4 beats per second with B = 320 Hz means
f_A = **316 Hz** or **324 Hz** ✓
**Step 2 — recall what filing does.** Filing **removes mass** from the prong, making it
stiffer relative to its mass, so the frequency **increases** ✓ (Loading a prong with wax
**lowers** it.)
**Step 3 — test f_A = 324 Hz.** Filing raises it to 325, 326, ... and the beat frequency
becomes **5, 6, ...** ✓ It could never return to 4. **Rejected** ✗
**Step 4 — test f_A = 316 Hz.** Filing raises it: the beats **fall** to 3, 2, 1, 0 as it
passes through 320, then **rise** again to 4 when it reaches **324 Hz** ✓ Consistent.
**Step 5 — conclude.** f_A before filing = **316 Hz** ✓
**The beat formula.**
beat frequency = **|f₁ − f₂|** ✓ the modulus, which is why 4 beats admits two
possibilities and a second observation is needed to choose between them.
**Why filing raises the frequency.** For a tuning fork,
f ∝ **t/l²** ✓ with t the prong thickness and l its length. Filing the **tip** shortens
l and raises f; filing the **inside of the prong** thins it and lowers f. The standard
convention - and the one intended here - is filing the tips.
**The trick of this question.** Both the before and after beat frequencies are **4** ✓
so the fork must have moved from 4 below to 4 above - passing exactly through B's
frequency on the way. That is possible only from 316 Hz.
**How beats are heard.** The two waves alternately reinforce and cancel ✓ producing a
slow throbbing at the **difference** frequency. The ear can follow beats up to about
10 per second; faster than that they merge into roughness.
**Why beats are useful.** They detect frequency differences of a fraction of a hertz ✓
which is why a piano tuner works by **eliminating** beats rather than by measuring
frequencies.
**The amplitude envelope.** Superposing two equal waves gives
y = 2a cos(π(f₁ − f₂)t) sin(π(f₁ + f₂)t) ✓ a carrier at the **mean** frequency, 318 Hz
here, modulated at the **difference**. The ear hears 2 maxima per cycle of the cosine,
hence 4 beats per second for a 4 Hz difference.
**Reading the distractors.** **324 Hz** ✗ is the frequency **after** filing - the
plausible trap. **328 Hz** ✗ would give 8 beats, and **320 Hz** ✗ none at all ✓
∴ 316 Hz.

Loudness follows **intensity**; pitch follows **frequency**.
**Step 1 — loudness.** The sensation of how strong a sound is ✓ determined by the energy
the wave carries, I ∝ **a²** - the **intensity**.
**Step 2 — pitch.** The sensation of how high or low a note is ✓ determined by the
**frequency**.
**Step 3 — conclude.** **Intensity and frequency** ✓
**The third characteristic, for completeness.** **Quality**, or timbre, is set by the
**harmonics** present and their relative strengths ✓ It is what distinguishes a violin
from a clarinet at the same pitch and loudness - and it is the answer to a different
question, which is why "frequency and number of harmonics" appears among the options.
**Why velocity cannot be the answer to either.** In air the speed depends only on
**temperature** ✓
v = 331√(T/273) m s⁻¹
so every note travels at the same speed. A sound that changed pitch or loudness with
speed would make music impossible at a distance.
**How intensity falls with distance.**
I ∝ **1/r²** ✓ for a point source, so doubling the distance quarters the intensity -
a drop of **6 dB**, which is a clearly audible reduction but far from inaudibility.
**Why the decibel scale is used.** The ear spans intensities from 10⁻¹² to 1 W m⁻² -
**twelve** orders of magnitude ✓ A logarithmic scale compresses that into 0 to 120 dB,
and matches the ear's own roughly logarithmic response.
**Some reference levels.** Whisper **30 dB**, conversation **60 dB**, traffic **80 dB**,
threshold of pain **120 dB** ✓
**The relation between pitch and wavelength.** v = fλ ✓ so at 340 m s⁻¹, middle C at
262 Hz has λ = **1·3 m** - which is why bass notes need large instruments and large
loudspeakers.
**Why the same note sounds different on different instruments.** The **fundamental** is
the same, fixing the pitch; the overtones differ, fixing the quality ✓ A flute is nearly
pure; a violin is rich in harmonics.
**Why the ear is not a simple intensity meter.** Equal-loudness contours show that a
100 Hz tone needs about **25 dB** more intensity than a 3 kHz tone to sound equally
loud ✓ Loudness is a sensation, intensity a physical quantity - related but not
identical.
∴ intensity and frequency.
